conventions.convention: θ is a unit line normal, θ⊥ = (−θ₂, θ₁), and the Fourier phase is exp(−2πi x·ξ).

The visibility definition assumes a nonempty proper open antipodally symmetric normal set with an open arc outside its closure. Nonzero covectors are visible exactly when their unit directions belong to Θ; WΘ excludes zero.

Schwartz Radon integrals use Lebesgue measure. Countable Choice is assumed for their agreement with compact-support Riemann line integrals; compact-support uniqueness is separately stated without Countable Choice.

The instability estimate uses complex-valued smooth functions, Lebesgue H¹ and object L² norms, arc-length angular measure, and Lebesgue offset measure. Its modulation sequence starts at N = 1 and requires infθ∈Θ |v·θ⊥| > 0.

The open problem concerns deterministic adversarial L² noise and arbitrary reconstruction functions, over compactly supported smooth inputs in the specified H¹ ball; its statistical comparison concerns different weighted spaces and spectral ellipsoids.

load_bearing.statement: Let Θ ⊂ S¹ be a nonempty open set of unit line normals and let f ∈ C_c^∞(R²; C). If the line integral Rf(θ,s) is zero for every θ ∈ Θ and s ∈ R, then f is zero everywhere. The assertion holds without Countable Choice.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every f ∈ S(R²), θ ∈ S¹, and σ ∈ R, the one-dimensional Fourier transform in the offset variable, using the phase exp(−2πi sσ), satisfies the Fourier-slice identity with the two-dimensional transform using exp(−2πi x·ξ). On compactly supported smooth inputs the formula has the same line parameterization and normalization as the Euclidean Radon transform.

For every f ∈ S(R²) and every θ ∈ S¹, the defining line integral converges absolutely for every real offset, and its offset function belongs to S(R). For each pair of nonnegative integers k,N, its kth derivative is bounded by Cₖ,ₙ(1+|s|)^(−N), with a finite constant independent of s and θ.

For f ∈ C_c^∞(R²; C), its compact-support Riemann Fourier-Laplace integral is independent of the containing rectangle, is entire in each complex coordinate, has coordinate derivatives obtained by inserting −2πi x_j into the integrand, and restricts to the stated Fourier transform on real frequencies. The proof uses no Countable Choice.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For a nonempty bounded open Ω ⊂ R², measurable Θ ⊂ S¹, and f ∈ C_c^∞(Ω; C), restricted Radon data belong to L²(Θ × R) and their squared norm is at most diam(Ω)|Θ| times the squared object L² norm.

concerns.concern: Proof 2.1 says the expansion of (θ⊥·∇)^m has 'all coefficients ... bounded by one'. In the collected multi-index expansion, binomial factors occur: for m = 3 and θ⊥ = (1/√2,1/√2), the mixed-derivative coefficient is 3/(2√2) > 1. Uniform bounds depending on m suffice for the claimed C_m estimate; alternatively the expansion can explicitly retain ordered derivative terms.

Proof 2.1 introduces approximating complex polynomials p_j and takes a sequential limit while emphasizing that no Countable Choice is used. The cited Stone-Weierstrass statement supplies an approximant for each positive error, without supplying a sequence. The argument closes choice-free by using one arbitrary ε-approximant at a time, or by specifying a canonical selection from rational-coefficient polynomials.

seams_checked.note: The open problem uses the deterministic stability framework faithfully. The null-function example applies the actual two-truth theorem with shared datum zero and an inclusion target map; that theorem does not require the target map to be onto the ambient L² target space.

The compact-support supplier uses Riemann integrals and the same negative-sign 2π phase and normal convention. Consumers retain its smooth compact-support domain; the Schwartz extension is proved separately with the stated Countable Choice assumptions.

Checked the requiring page and its companion missing-angle covector example, the actual item citation. Its conormal calculation gives ξ = τθ; antipodal symmetry therefore makes the absence of a canonical pair equivalent to the cited invisible-direction condition. Its diagram agrees with that convention.
